title: Laboratory: turn a tree ensemble into a vector

what.formal: This laboratory runs Equations (4) through (9) on the two-tree ensemble of Figure 2. It computes the content bits $\mu_c$ by testing every inner-node predicate against the vertex's features, the position weights $\mu_p = \alpha/(d(o)+\beta)$ from each node's depth, the per-tree block $\varphi_r^i$ as their product, the concatenated row $X_r$, and finally the fused vector $Z = (X_s \odot X_r) \Vert X_r$ with $X_s$ fixed at $0.9526$ for display.
what.plain: Slide three feature values and two weighting knobs, and watch each question in a two-tree ensemble turn into a number — then watch those numbers become the vector the network actually receives.

what.md: **What to look for.** Three things. First, that a **satisfied** question contributes **zero** — the inverted convention from Equation (5), which is the single easiest thing to get backwards. Second, that the nonzero entries are exactly the **depth weights** of the questions that failed, so the vector's magnitudes come from a small set rather than a continuum. Third, that the fused vector $Z$ is always **twice** as wide as $X_r$, and that its first half is the second half scaled by the same number for a given vertex.

**$X_s$ is held fixed here.** A real vertex's structural value comes from its degree through Equation (3), which needs the hypergraph — this laboratory isolates the rule side, so the structural factor is pinned at one value to keep the arithmetic visible. The scaling behaviour is what matters: multiply any entry of the first half by $1/0.9526$ and you recover the corresponding entry of the second half.

example.md: **Task 1 — reproduce the walkthrough.** Leave everything at its default: $x_1 = 3$, $x_2 = 5$, $x_3 = 7$, $\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 1$.

items.md: Read the five chips. Every question should be marked *covered*, because 3, 5 and 7 satisfy all five thresholds.
items.why: Five questions, five chips — and the chip list is the encoding's table of contents. Its length is $C_r$, the width of the rule embedding.

items.md: Read $X_r$. It should be all zeros.
items.why: **This is the inverted convention in its most extreme form.** A vertex the ensemble explains completely has no failures to record, so its entire rule row is zero — and therefore, via Equation (9), so is its fused vector. Card 69 explains why the paper's encoding has this property and why it is essentially unreachable with a large ensemble.
The doubling is the concatenation. Note that $X_r$ and the scaled copy are both five entries wide, so $Z$ is ten — the paper's $2C_r$.

example.md: **Task 2 — make some questions fail.** Move $x_1$ down to 0, leaving $x_2 = 5$ and $x_3 = 7$. The sliders start at $\alpha = \beta = 6$, the middle of the paper's searched range.

items.md: See which chips flip to *not covered*: the two that depend on $x_1$, namely $x_1 \ge 1$ at depth 1 and $x_1 \ge 2$ at depth 1.
items.why: Two questions fail out of five, and they are in different trees — evidence that the questionnaire spans the ensemble rather than following one tree's path.

items.md: Read $X_r$ and note which entries are nonzero and what their values are: $0.500$ in positions 2 and 4, and zero elsewhere.
items.why: Both failing questions sit at depth 1, so both carry the weight $\mu_p = 1/(1+1) = 0.5$. **The nonzero values are exactly the depth weights of the failed questions** — the vector takes its magnitudes from a small discrete set, never from a continuum.

items.md: Now move $x_2$ down to 0 as well. The root question $x_2 \ge 2$ at depth 0 also fails, and its entry becomes $1.000$.
items.why: Failing a root question costs twice what failing a depth-1 question costs. This is the depth weighting doing its job, and it is the mechanism by which the encoding expresses that some questions matter more.

example.md: **Task 3 — separate the two knobs.** With $x_1 = 0$, $x_2 = 0$, $x_3 = 7$ so that three questions fail at depths 0, 1 and 1, vary $\alpha$ and then $\beta$.

items.md: Watch the pattern while moving only $\alpha$: every nonzero entry scales by the same factor.
items.why: $\alpha$ multiplies the whole weighting. The relative standing of the root question against the deeper ones does not move — so $\alpha$ cannot change *which* question dominates.

items.md: Now 1 and vary only $\beta$ from 1 to 2, then to 0.5.
items.why: At $\beta = 2$ the root's weight falls to $0.5$ and the depth-1 questions to $0.333$ — the gap narrows. At $\beta = 0.5$ the root weighs $2.0$ against the depth-1 weight $0.667$ — the gap widens. **$\beta$ is the knob that expresses how strongly the authors believe the root matters more**, and it is the one the paper never reports.

example.md: **Task 4 — watch the fusion's structure.** With a nonzero $X_r$, compare the two vector rows on screen.

Pick any nonzero entry of $\tilde{X}_r$ and divide it by the corresponding entry of $X_r$. You get $0.9526$ every time — the structural scalar, applied to the whole row at once. **That is the fusion's exact behaviour**: one number per vertex reweights every rule slot identically. It cannot make one rule count more than another, and it cannot amplify, because $0.9526 < 1$. Both facts follow from the shapes, and both are visible here in a way they are not in the equations.

quiz.q: A vertex satisfies every question in both trees. What does $X_r$ look like?

opts.expl: Ones would be the convention where 1 means satisfied. The paper uses the opposite convention, and this is exactly the trap it sets.

Correct. A satisfied question contributes $\mu_p(o) \times 0 = 0$. A fully explained vertex therefore has an all-zero rule row, and consequently an all-zero fused vector. This is the extreme case of the inverted convention, and the laboratory lets you produce it by leaving the sliders at their defaults.

opts.md: All equal to the root's weight
opts.expl: The weights enter only where the bit is 1. A satisfied question has bit 0, so its weight is multiplied away — nothing survives.

quiz.q: With $\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 1$ and $x_1 = 0$, $x_2 = 5$, $x_3 = 7$, how many entries of $X_r$ are nonzero?
quiz.hint: Count the questions the feature values fail — not the ones they satisfy.
quiz.sol: Two. With $x_1 = 0$ the questions $x_1 \ge 1$ and $x_1 \ge 2$ both fail, contributing their depth weights; $x_2 = 5$ and $x_3 = 7$ satisfy everything else, contributing zero. So $X_r = (0,\; 0.5,\; 0,\; 0.5,\; 0)$. Answering 3 counts the satisfied questions instead, which inverts the convention.

quiz.q: Which statements about the fused vector $Z$ are true for every vertex?

opts.md: It is twice as wide as $X_r$
opts.expl: Right — the concatenation joins two blocks of the same width, so $Z \in \mathbb{R}^{2C_r}$ always.

opts.md: Its first half equals its second half
opts.expl: That would be the degenerate case. The first half is the second half *multiplied by the structural scalar*, so the two halves differ whenever that scalar differs from 1 — and it always does, since it comes from a sigmoid.

opts.md: Every entry of its first half has smaller magnitude than the corresponding entry of its second half
opts.expl: Right, whenever the rule entry is nonzero. The structural scalar lies strictly in $(0,1)$, so it shrinks everything it touches. This is the range fact from Equation (9)'s card, and it is why the word "amplified" in the paper's own description should be read as a relative statement.

opts.md: It can distinguish two rule slots of the same vertex
opts.expl: It cannot. One scalar per vertex multiplies the whole row, so the relative sizes of a vertex's rule entries are preserved exactly. Distinguishing one slot from another would need a structural embedding with one value per slot, which this design does not have.
